gotcha_text: Landlords often exploit vague maintenance definitions to pass the cost of major structural replacements directly to medical tenants. This creates massive, unbudgeted spikes in operating expenses that can devastate a practice's annual cash flow.
fix_text: Tenant Pulse flags ambiguous 'repair' language and identifies where capital improvements lack necessary amortization clauses. Our tool generates precise legal language to ensure structural upgrades are spread over their useful life.
deep_dive_html:
The Perils of Unregulated Operating Expenses

For medical practices, predictability is the cornerstone of financial stability. However, Common Area Maintenance (CAM) clauses are frequently drafted as catch-all provisions that allow landlords to pass through nearly any building-related cost to the tenant. The most insidious trap lies in the conflated definition of maintenance versus capital improvements. A sophisticated landlord will attempt to categorize structural replacements—such as a full HVAC overhaul or parking lot reconstruction—as mere repairs to ensure they can be recovered immediately through your monthly CAM charges.

Beyond structural costs, medical tenants are often blindsided by administrative fees and management fees that are calculated as a percentage of total operating expenses. Without a hard cap, these fees become a compounding drain on your practice's revenue, effectively allowing the landlord to increase their profit margin under the guise of operational necessity.

Securing Market-Standard Protections

To protect your practice, your lease must distinguish between routine maintenance and capital expenditures. A robust lease agreement should mandate that any capital improvement that provides a long-term benefit to the property must be amortized over its useful life, with only the annual amortized portion included in your CAM obligations. This prevents a single, massive, unbudgeted expense from crippling your cash flow in a single fiscal year.

    Administrative Fee Caps: Limit management and administrative fees to a fixed percentage, typically between 5% and 15%, of total operating expenses.

    Expense Caps: Implement a cap on controllable expenses, ensuring that year-over-year increases in non-tax and non-insurance items do not exceed a set percentage, such as 5%.

    Exclusion of Capital Costs: Explicitly exclude any costs related to the replacement of structural elements or major systems unless they are strictly categorized as repairs and are amortized over their useful life.

title: Hidden Traps in Common Area Maintenance Clauses for Medical Practices
